narrative:
The model determined that you have a 91% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school sets a high bar for admission and this predicted failure risk is so high, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were by far the strongest influences. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of accepted students who typically ranked around the middle of their class. These unusually low rankings strongly pushed the model toward predicting that you would fail the bar exam. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.10 also worked against you, though to a lesser degree. It fell slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted applicants and nudged the prediction further toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 30, compared to an average of 37 among accepted students, added to the concern, as did your middle-income background. However, these were not the dominant reasons for the rejection. Gender and race played no role in the model’s decision.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Building a stronger record in these areas will help demonstrate your readiness for law school and the bar exam in future applications. (218 words)
